summary:
Hii!!! I made a small 3D game you play in the browser (on computer), about a boy and his little robot. His mom was an astronaut, and since she left for the stars, it's just the two of them. She left him her ship, and a promise that one day they would go up there together. So he goes.

You help him get the ship ready, and that's where the Space Mission Design part comes in. You choose the launcher, fuel, shielding, power, a science camera, an antenna and a tether, and you have to make it all fit in the budget, the launcher's weight limit and your power supply. Then you fly it, and every choice follows you into space: solar flares, Earth's shadow, meteoroids, a spacewalk, a Moon landing. A report at the end tells you what each choice did and why.

I think it matters because mission trade-offs usually feel like a table of numbers. When you care about the person in the ship, you feel them. And each mission ends with a real NASA photo of Earth, which I wanted to feel like a gift.
details:
Let's talk details!
What it does and how it works

In the hangar you build the ship yourself. You pick the launcher, the fuel, the shielding, the power system, a science camera, an antenna, and the tether for the spacewalk. Everything costs money, everything adds weight, and the camera and antenna need power. Little bars show you right away when you go too far: budget, weight, power, how much of your data will really reach Earth, and whether you have enough fuel.

And you can't have everything. If you want the best science, you need the big antenna, or half your data never makes it home, and extra solar panels to power it all. The only way it fits the budget is to fly without a shield. So you choose between science and safety, like real mission teams do.

Then you fly what you built. A solar flare hurts more if you skipped the shield. In Earth's shadow the solar panels stop, and without a battery the engines slow down. On the spacewalk, a longer tether gives you more tries to reach the satellite. Behind the Moon you lose the radio no matter what, the same thing that happened to Apollo 8 in 1968. If the ship is too heavy or runs out of fuel, the ship's computer tells you what went wrong and you go back and fix it. After each mission there's a report card: a score out of 100, and one line for each choice explaining what it did.

You can play alone or with up to 4 friends on one screen. Each person gets a role (mission lead, engineering, science, communications), and nobody launches until everyone agrees, so you have to talk it out.

The benefits

You learn the "why," not just the answer. Under every part there's one simple sentence about why it matters in real life, each report ends with a "Did you know?", and there's a small arcade with a gallery of famous NASA photos and a memory game where every pair teaches you a fact. It works in French and English, in any browser, with nothing to install.

The impact I hope for

I want kids and beginners to understand that designing a mission is about choices and compromises, and that failing and trying again is part of it. And I hope someone reaches the last screen, picks a date that means something to them, and sees NASA's real photo of Earth from that day.

Tools and languages

JavaScript and Three.js for the 3D, HTML and CSS, hosted on Vercel, code on GitHub. I designed the astronaut in Blender. The crying you hear on the Moon is me, I recorded it myself; the other sounds and the music are made in code with the Web Audio API. NASA data comes from the EPIC API (DSCOVR) and the NASA Image and Video Library. I wrote the base code and the story, and AI (Claude) supported me: it helped fix and clean up my code, smooth the animations, add some features after I playtested, and write the French and English dialogue from my story.

What makes it creative

Most mission games start with the rocket. Mine starts with a feeling. The NASA photos aren't decoration, they're what the whole story is walking toward: the satellite sends back today's Earth, on the Moon he takes Earthrise, and at the end the game asks you which day you'd like to see Earth again.

What I considered

I wanted it to be fair for beginners, so after two crashes the game offers an easy mode. I wanted no single "right" ship, so the budget forces a real choice. I wanted it to be honest, so the radio blackout behind the Moon can't be fixed by any antenna, just like in real life. And I wanted it short, about 5 to 7 minutes, so anyone can reach the ending.
